experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/ti: Sadhu Sundar Singh's vision of Christ
experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/ac: Paraphrase of Sundar Singh's own testimony as recorded by Streeter and Appasamy: a fifteen-year-old Sikh boy, grieving his mother's death and hostile to Christianity (he publicly burned a Bible), prayed through the night of 18 December 1904 resolved to die on the railway line before the morning train unless God revealed himself. Before dawn a light filled his room and he saw the figure of Jesus with nail-pierced hands, who spoke to him in Hindustani. Baptised in the Anglican church in Shimla in 1905, he became a wandering Christian sadhu in saffron robes, travelling across India and into Tibet.
experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/co: His vision and ascetic Indian style made him famous in Europe in the 1920s. He disappeared on a journey into Tibet in 1929. Some European critics (the Jesuit Fr Hosten and the psychoanalyst Oskar Pfister, 1926) questioned miracle stories in his travels, such as a 300-year-old 'Maharishi of Kailash'.
experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/as: Celebrated as a pioneer of indigenous Indian Christianity who showed that faith in Christ need not mean Westernisation.
Respected as a mystic; some Catholic critics in his day investigated and disputed specific miracle claims.
His visions are often cited as examples of direct revelation of Christ to people of other faiths, a theme recurring in reports from the Muslim world.
Pfister's psychoanalytic study and later scholars debate how to read his visions; his conversion account is consistent and first-hand, while the later travel miracles are less corroborated.
experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/st:
Sundar Singh was born in 1889 into a wealthy Sikh family in the village of Rampur, in the Ludhiana district of the Punjab. His mother was deeply religious and took him to Sikh holy places and to Hindu ascetics (sadhus), and he learned scriptures from Sikh and Hindu traditions. He also attended a school run by American Presbyterian missionaries, where the Bible was taught, which he resented.

When he was fourteen his mother died, and he was overwhelmed by grief and spiritual restlessness. According to his own later account, in his anger he tore up and publicly burned a copy of the Gospels, and he threw stones at Christian preachers. In December 1904, he said, he resolved to find peace or die: he would pray through the night, and if God did not reveal himself by morning he would throw himself in front of the early train that passed near his home.

On the night of 18 December 1904 he prayed, according to his testimony, to whatever God might exist. Before dawn, he said, a bright light filled the room, and he saw the figure of Jesus, whom he recognised from pictures and from the Gospels, with the marks of the nails in his hands. He reported that Jesus spoke to him in Hindustani, asking why he persecuted him, and that he was filled with peace. He woke his father and told him he had become a follower of Jesus.

His family tried to dissuade him with persuasion, inducements and threats. According to his account, he was eventually driven from home, and food given to him on his departure had been poisoned, from which he recovered with the help of Christians. He went to the mission at Ludhiana, and on his sixteenth birthday, 3 September 1905, he was baptised at St Thomas's Anglican Church in Shimla.

Soon afterwards he adopted the saffron robe of a Hindu sadhu, believing that Indians would better understand Christ through a familiar form of holy life. He travelled on foot through the Punjab, Kashmir and the Himalayas, owning almost nothing, and repeatedly crossed into Tibet, where Christian preaching was forbidden. He briefly studied at St John's Divinity College in Lahore and received a preaching licence, but later gave it up to remain free of denominational ties. Stories circulated, many from his own lips, of persecution and miraculous deliverance in Tibet, including being thrown into a dry well and rescued by an unknown helper, and of meeting a Christian hermit hundreds of years old, the 'Maharishi of Kailash'.

From 1918 he made speaking tours across India, Ceylon, Malaya, China and Japan, and in 1920 and 1922 visited Britain, the United States, Australia and continental Europe, where large audiences were drawn by his calm, simple teaching and parable-like style. The theologian B.H. Streeter and A.J. Appasamy published a study of his spirituality in 1921, and his own short books, such as At the Master's Feet, were widely translated. Controversy followed: in the mid-1920s the Jesuit H. Hosten and the Swiss pastor and psychoanalyst Oskar Pfister argued that some of his travel and miracle stories were unverified or untrue, while the scholar Friedrich Heiler defended him. In April 1929 Sundar Singh set out once more for Tibet and was never seen again.

experiences/sadhu-sundar-singh-vision/si: Sadhu Sundar Singh became the best-known Indian Christian of his generation and a pioneer of expressing faith in Christ through Indian forms of holiness rather than European church culture, an approach later developed in Indian Christian ashrams and theology. His conversion through a vision, without human preaching, is frequently cited in discussions of dreams and visions of Christ among people of other faiths. The controversy over his travel stories made him a test case for evaluating testimony and hagiography in modern times. He remains widely read in India and beyond, and is commemorated in some Anglican calendars.
experiences/john-sung-revival-campaigns/: John Sung's revival and healing campaigns in China and Southeast Asia
Shanghai (Bethel Mission)

Paraphrase of Sung's diaries and Lian Xi's study: John Sung (Song Shangjie), a Fujianese pastor's son with a PhD in chemistry from Ohio State University, experienced a dramatic conversion in New York in 1927 and was confined for six months in a psychiatric hospital before returning to China. From 1931 with the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band, and independently from 1933, he preached across China and among Chinese in the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies until about 1940, with intense calls to repentance, dramatic gestures and healing services in which thousands reported cures.

Admirers called him the 'Wesley of China'; Chinese Christians credited him with planting hundreds of preaching bands. Critics, including some missionaries, disliked his harshness and theatrical methods. He died of tuberculosis in 1944.
Chinese evangelical / house church
A spiritual father of independent Chinese Protestantism whose emphasis on repentance, Bible and evangelistic bands influenced later house churches.
Mainline mission
Some missionaries criticised his anti-modernist polemics and emotional style but acknowledged his effectiveness.
Historian
Lian Xi places Sung within the rise of an indigenous, millenarian popular Protestantism in Republican China.

His 1927 hospitalisation is variously read as a breakdown, a misunderstood conversion crisis or both.

John Sung (Song Shangjie) was born in 1901 in Hinghwa (Putian), Fujian province, the son of a Methodist pastor. As a boy he was affected by a local revival in 1909 and became known as a 'little pastor' for his preaching. In 1919 he went to the United States to study, earning degrees at Ohio Wesleyan University and Ohio State University, where he received a PhD in chemistry in 1926. He then enrolled at Union Theological Seminary in New York, where liberal theology threw his faith into crisis.

According to his diaries, in February 1927, after a period of spiritual turmoil, he experienced an intense conversion: a vision of Christ, a sense of total forgiveness, and a call to preach. His behaviour became so extreme, including fervent public preaching and declarations that alarmed the seminary, that he was committed to a psychiatric hospital in New York, where he remained for about six months. He later described this as a time of deep Bible study. After his release he sailed for China in late 1927; according to a well-known story, he threw his academic certificates into the sea, keeping only his doctoral diploma for his father.

Back in Fujian he taught and preached, and in 1931 he joined the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band, organised by the Bethel Mission in Shanghai, a mission led by the American missionary Jennie Hughes and the Chinese physician Mary Stone (Shi Meiyu). With Andrew Gih (Ji Zhiwen) and others, the band travelled thousands of miles across China, holding revival meetings in churches of many denominations. In 1933-34 Sung parted from Bethel and continued independently.

His preaching was unforgettable. Witnesses describe him running across the platform, using props such as a coffin to illustrate death to sin, singing songs he had composed, and naming specific sins of church members and pastors, demanding public confession and restitution. Meetings often lasted many hours over several days. Healing services became part of his campaigns: he prayed over long lines of sick people, and thousands reported cures. He organised converts into 'preaching bands' of three or more lay people who went out weekly to evangelise, and emphasised Bible study.

From 1935 he travelled extensively among the Chinese diaspora of South-East Asia, in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya, Thailand, Taiwan and the Dutch East Indies, where many churches date their growth to his visits. Critics, including some missionaries and Chinese church leaders, objected to his harshness, his public attacks on clergy, his emotionalism and his theatrical methods; some questioned the healing claims. The historian Lian Xi has analysed him as a central figure in the rise of a fervent, independent Chinese Christianity with apocalyptic and charismatic tendencies.

By 1940 his health was failing from tuberculosis and other illness, and he spent his final years largely bedridden in Beijing, writing and praying, during the Japanese occupation. He died on 18 August 1944, aged 42.

John Sung is widely regarded as the most influential Chinese evangelist of the twentieth century, and his campaigns in China and South-East Asia shaped generations of Chinese churches, preachers and lay preaching bands. His fervent, Bible-centred and often charismatic style foreshadowed the independent Chinese Christianity that later grew in house churches after missionaries left. Critics, then and now, question his methods, the verification of healings and his harsh public denunciations. His story also raises questions about the boundary between intense religious experience and mental illness, as his own psychiatric confinement shows.
